attacks.claim: The plan targets reason #2 (22%) but ignores the top churn reason, 'too much setup / typing' (38%). It then adds heavy setup: 15 items, each with quantity, unit and expiry, before any value is delivered. This worsens the biggest churn driver and will likely crater unlock rates.
attacks.evidence: "unlocks once a user has entered at least 15 items with expiry dates" vs. "Too much setup / typing to get useful suggestions — 38%"

attacks.claim: The success target of 25% of MAU unlocking within 60 days is implausible and unsupported. Sizing assumes only 30% of MAU create a pantry in 90 days, and the unlock bar (15 items with expiry) is far higher than creating a pantry. The metrics contradict the sizing assumption and the friction gate. No prototype or evidence shows users will enter 15 dated items.
attacks.evidence: "25% of MAU unlock Pantry Match within 60 days" vs. "30% of MAU create a pantry within 90 days"

attacks.claim: The nightly job scores all 340k recipes for every pantry user in a single SQL statement on the primary. At the 30% adoption assumption (~630k users) versus the 12k tested, that is ~52x the staging load. Linear extrapolation of 41 minutes gives ~36 hours, so it cannot finish in a nightly window. The cost is also O(users x recipes) and rescans users whose pantry did not change.
attacks.evidence: "12,000 synthetic pantry users completed in 41 minutes"; "score every recipe in the catalog (340k recipes) in a single SQL statement ... on the primary"

attacks.claim: A giant long-running join on the single write primary risks lock contention, replication lag, and bloat from mass upserts, degrading the whole app. The job has no batching, checkpointing, timeout, retry/resume or alerting. A failure mid-run leaves stale or partial pantry_matches. Staging used synthetic data and was not at production scale.
attacks.evidence: "single SQL statement joining pantry_items x recipe_ingredients on the primary, then upsert the top 50"

attacks.claim: The pantry_matches table grows to ~31M rows (630k users x 50) and is rewritten nightly. No retention policy exists for churned or inactive users, so the job keeps computing for them.
attacks.evidence: "top 50 per user"; "for each user with a pantry"

attacks.claim: The scoring ignores quantity and unit even though they are collected, so a recipe needing 2 cups of flour matches a user holding a pinch. Expired items are not excluded, and the score favours recipes with few ingredients. Dietary restrictions and allergens are not mentioned in filtering. Staples being 'always present' may also mis-score recipes built around oil or pepper.
attacks.evidence: "Score = (pantry ingredients used / recipe ingredients) weighted by expiry proximity"

attacks.claim: Recurring maintenance burden: users must manually update quantities after cooking, and items expire. Nothing handles stale pantries (no decay, no removal of items past expiry). Match quality will degrade and users will abandon. There are also no faster entry paths (barcode, receipt scan, bulk add, or a staples preset), which reinforces the typing friction.
attacks.evidence: "Users are asked to update quantities after cooking (prompt on the recipe 'I made this' screen)"

attacks.claim: Pantry contents with push notifications are new behavioural data, but retention, deletion on account removal, and analytics treatment are unspecified. The plan includes analytics events without stating what is captured.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: data retention/deletion policy for pantry_items and pantry_matches; "analytics events" unspecified

attacks.claim: The rollout goes from 5% beta to 100% within week 6 with no stated rollback criteria, kill switch, or guardrail metrics. The job and the table writes against the primary are hard to unwind once load is live.

The 6-week timeline compresses three platforms, the data model, the scoring job, the carousel, notifications and analytics. It allows no time for load testing at scale or for measuring beta results before 100% rollout. The retention success metric can't be read within a 30-day window in a 6-week plan.
attacks.evidence: "+3 pts 30-day retention for users who unlock vs. matched control"

attacks.claim: The plan does not address screen-reader accessibility for the progress bar, the expiry date picker, or autocomplete across three platforms.
